title: Bodh Gaya restored
hookLine: the temple at the place of awakening, restored and visited again

lines: A TALL TOWER AND AN OLD TREE.
ROBES OF EVERY COLOR, ONE TREE.
cards: Late afternoon in Bodh Gaya, in the state of Bihar in India. A tall, tapering temple tower rises over the town, and behind it, a wide, old tree with heart-shaped leaves. Under the tree, prayer flags.
On the stone railings, rows of butter lamps. Monks in maroon from the Himalayas sit beside monks in saffron from Thailand and nuns in gray from Korea.

Someone is chanting in Pali, someone in Tibetan, someone silently doing prostrations on a wooden board, again and again. A leaf falls, and three people move to pick it up. It wasn't always like this here.

teach.b: The Vinaya's own account of the awakening begins here: at Uruvela, on the bank of the Neranjara river, the newly awakened Buddha sits at the foot of the bodhi tree for seven days, taking in the joy of freedom.
Bodhi means awakening, and the tree is named for what happened under it. Second, the seat.

In the Anguttara Nikaya, the Buddha looks back on his striving and recalls his resolve: let only skin, sinews and bones remain, let flesh and blood dry up, he would not slacken his effort until he reached what effort could reach.
Tradition places that resolve here, under the tree. Pilgrims came.

teach.h: THE DIAMOND SEAT AND A RESOLVE.
teach.b: A great temple rose beside the tree, and a stone slab, the vajrasana, the diamond seat, marks where tradition says he sat.
Third, the long quiet. As Buddhism faded in India, the pilgrims thinned and the temple fell into neglect. Fourth, the return.
Restorers came, among them workers sent from Burma and, later, British archaeologists, who rebuilt and repaired the temple.
And tradition says the tree that grows there now descends from the very tree the Buddha sat under. Remember the cutting carried to Sri Lanka, the one tradition says still grows at Anuradhapura?

Some accounts say the line came back the other way too, from that tree to this one. So Buddhists of different schools, from different lands, sit under the same branches. Nobody owns the moment of awakening.
The tree just keeps growing, and people keep coming back to it.

how: Buddhist pilgrims come to the Mahabodhi Temple at Bodh Gaya to sit, chant, make offerings and walk clockwise around the temple and the bodhi tree, and some do long sets of prostrations there.

o: awakening; the tree is named for it
a fig leaf kept as a pilgrim's token
the stone seat where the Buddha sat

games.q: Bodh Gaya restored: tap the pairs.
p: where the Buddha sat and awoke
the diamond seat, a stone slab
let only skin, sinews and bones remain
workers from Burma, then British archaeologists

s: the Buddha awoke inside a great temple
he sat at the foot of a tree; the temple rose beside it later.
the temple at Bodh Gaya was always busy, without a break
as Buddhism faded in India, it fell quiet and into ruin before it was restored.
the Vinaya says the Buddha sat under the bodhi tree for seven days after awakening
at Uruvela, by the Neranjara river, taking in the joy of freedom.

games.q: you've just awakened at the foot of a tree at Uruvela, by the Neranjara river. what do you do next?
o: get up at once and set off to teach.
stay seated under the tree, taking in the joy of freedom.
go home to the palace to tell your family.
games.why: the Vinaya says he sat on at the foot of the bodhi tree for seven days, taking in the joy of freedom. the tree, and the place, still draw people back.

practice: Picture the wide trunk and the heart-shaped leaves moving in a warm breeze, the stone under you still warm from the day, and quiet voices around you in many languages, all turned toward the same tree.
Add nothing; just sit at its foot, the way the story says he did, and let the breath come and go.

wordCard.voice: Bodhi. Awakening; the tree at Bodh Gaya named for what happened beneath it, visited again after the temple fell quiet. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali and Sanskrit: awakening. the tree is named for what happened under it.

carryVoice: Your line: back to the tree. A place gone quiet can fill again. That's day eight hundred ninety-four.

sources.ref: Anguttara Nikaya 2.5 (the resolve: skin, sinews and bones)
